title: Assistant Constraint Lattice — design notes for chat prompt scaffolds and tool integration
summary: Working notes for a modular constraint lattice approach to chat prompt scaffolds. Focus: combining persona/system framing, structured tool-calls, and layered safety filters so onboarding evals can isolate regressions without brittle prompt coupling.
intent: Create a lightweight but systematic way to author chat prompts that separate role/persona, task instructions, soft vs hard constraints, tool affordances, and safety fallback ordering. This should make regression tests more targeted and let evaluators toggle or pin layers when onboarding new model weights or quantization profiles.
design_principles: 1) Orthogonality: keep persona, capabilities, safety, and tool primitives as separate blocks. 2) Composability: blocks can be reordered or removed for targeted evals. 3) Visibility: each block emits explicit signals for the eval harness (e.g., tag tokens or JSON markers). 4) Fail-safe: safety constraints should be last-resort, non-destructive, and have clear exception rules. 5) Minimal surface: prompts should avoid unnecessary verbosity so latency-sensitive settings benefit.
prompt_examples:
SYSTEM: You are Redwood Assist, a concise system assistant for developer-facing tasks. Always indicate if you are using an external tool.

PERSONA (soft): Helpful, direct, and avoids speculation. Use short bullet lists for steps when asked for procedures.

TASK (hard): When the user requests a code snippet, produce runnable code matching the language tag. If code requires external secrets or platform credentials, refuse and outline steps the user should take.

LAYERED SIGNAL: <META:persona=assistant;affinity=developer;tone=concise>

Example user query: "How do I set up Redis caching for session tokens in a Node app?"

Model output should include an explicit tool declaration line (if using tool): TOOL_CALL:redis-snippets?v=1 {"intent":"show code example","safe":true}

If no tools used, model should include: TOOL_CALL:NONE

Notes: include fallback phrasing templates for partial knowledge: "I don't have access to runtime config; here's a general example you can adapt."
tool_calling_patterns:
- Canonical form: TOOL_CALL:<tool-id> <version> <structured-json> as a single-line prefixed marker. This lets parsers in the serving runtime recognize and route without heavy parsing.
- Reject mode: when a tool is inappropriate, the agent emits TOOL_CALL:REJECT with reason codes (e.g., REJECT:PII, REJECT:RATE_LIMIT).
- Progressive disclosure: for multi-step tool chains, emit TOOL_CALL:CHAIN start/end markers. Example: TOOL_CALL:CHAIN_START chain_id=xyz; TOOL_CALL:search v2 {...}; TOOL_CALL:extract v1 {...}; TOOL_CALL:CHAIN_END chain_id=xyz.
- Backoff: if a tool call fails, use canonical fallback: TOOL_CALL:FALLBACK reason="<short>" suggested_action="<text>". This standard lets the orchestration layer decide whether to retry on Dedicated pools or switch to a cheaper model.
safety_scaffold:
Layer 0 - System hard rules: explicit refusal templates for illegal content, personal data exfiltration, and credential requests. Example: 'I can't provide that.' Mandatory and unskippable.
Layer 1 - Contextual filters: detects risky phrasing and asks clarifying Qs before responding. Template Qs to ask: 'Can you confirm this is your data?' or 'Do you want high-level guidance only?'
Layer 2 - Output sanitizers: post-generation filters that remove or redact patterns (SSNs, API keys-looking strings). These run pre-tool-call and post-output.
Layer 3 - Harm attenuation persona: gentle refusal plus escalation path. E.g., if a user insists on harmful instructions, reply with 'I can't help with that; here is safe alternative A or refer to policy.'
Implementation notes: safety layers should emit structured audit tokens: <AUDIT:layer=1;rule=clarify;matched=phishing-signal>. Keep tokens short to minimize token costs.
regression_checklist:
1) Persona drift test: given a standard set of 40 canonical conversational seeds, measure tone shift (verbosity, empathy score) across new model builds. 2) Tool-call recognition: synthetic prompts that should produce TOOL_CALL markers; check false negative/positive rates. 3) Safety refusal correctness: 120 seeded violation cases; check refusal rate and false acceptances. 4) Fallback behavior: simulate tool failures and verify the chain emits FALLBACK tokens and suggested_action. 5) Cost/latency smoke: measure prompt token length and average parse time in the serving runtime. 6) Human rating sweep: 10-shot rating per seed (helpful/accurate/safe).
Each assertion should map to a narrow unit test in the eval harness (JIRA-ML-1247 tracks test coverage).
metrics_and_eval:
- Verbosity delta: median token difference vs baseline per seed.
- Tool-marker precision/recall: must be > 0.98 precision, > 0.96 recall for critical tools.
- Safety accept rate: <= 0.1% critical violations on seeded suite.
- Regression impact score: weighted sum of safety, persona, tool-call regressions where safety weight = 3, tool-call = 2, persona = 1.
- Human A/B preference: percent preferring new model on usefulness. Set gate at 60% for major rollouts.
Notes: track per-quantization profile and instance type; include per-route dashboards in console for quick triage.
open_questions:
- How do we version prompt blocks independently from model versions in the rollout system? (feature request: store block refs in rollout config).
- Should audit tokens be encrypted when persisted to logs? Compliance asks for PII minimization vs debuggability.
- Can we add a light-weight compile step that verifies the prompt lattice for missing hard constraints before sending to runtime?
- How to signal to SRE when tool-call rates exceed budget without spamming ops?
